lede: Two ways a cell can divide. One makes a copy, for growing and healing. The other makes gametes, and halves the chromosome number on the way. Almost every mark in this topic comes from four numbers: how many divisions, how many cells, how many chromosomes, and how alike they are.
can: Give the four numbers for mitosis and for meiosis without swapping them.
Choose the nuclei meiosis could produce from a set of diagrams.
Explain why gametes must be haploid and name what makes them different.

md: Cells wear out, wounds close, and you grew from a single cell. All of that is one kind of division. A second, different kind happens in only two organs, and it is why no two of us are alike.

md:
**Mitosis** copies a cell. The chromosomes are duplicated exactly, then the cell divides **once**, giving **two** daughter cells.

Each daughter cell has the **same number** of chromosomes as the parent and the **same genes**, so it is a **clone** of it.

Nothing is halved. A body cell with 46 chromosomes gives two cells with 46 each.

prompt: One cell divides by mitosis. How many daughter cells are produced?
explain: 2. One division of the nucleus gives two cells, and they are clones of the parent.

md:
**Meiosis** is a **reduction division**: the nucleus divides **twice** and one cell becomes **four**.

Each of the four is **haploid** — it holds **half** the parent's chromosome number, one out of every pair — and all four are **genetically different** from one another.

A cell in an ovary with 46 chromosomes makes four ova with 23 each.

prompt: One cell divides by meiosis. How many daughter cells are produced?
explain: 4. Two divisions of the nucleus, so four cells — and each holds half the chromosome number.

title: Worked example: a fruit fly has 8 chromosomes in a body cell. How many are in one of its sperm cells? [2]
md:
**Step 1 — name the division.** Sperm cells are gametes, and gametes are made by **meiosis**. **[1]**
**Step 2 — halve, because meiosis is a reduction division.** 8 ÷ 2 = **4**. **[1]**

The check that catches most slips: two gametes join at fertilisation, so 4 + 4 = 8 takes you back to a body cell. If your number does not do that, it is wrong.

prompt: A human body cell holds 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in one human ovum?
explain: 23. Meiosis halves the number, and 23 + 23 at fertilisation gives 46 again.

text: 5. Choosing the nuclei meiosis could make

alt: A parent cell holding a long pair and a short pair of chromosomes, then six numbered nuclei, (i) to (vi), each holding a different selection of those chromosomes. A shaded chromosome came from one parent and a clear one from the other; the pair of long chromosomes and the pair of short chromosomes are the two functional pairs. The three nuclei that meiosis could produce, (i), (iii), (vi), are ringed.
caption: One of each pair, in any combination. Nothing more, nothing less.

md:
The parent cell holds two pairs: a long pair and a short pair. A cell made by meiosis must hold **one of each pair** — one long and one short — and it does not matter which one of each.

So test every nucleus with two questions. Exactly one long? Exactly one short? Here that rules in (i), (iii), (vi) and rules out the rest.

title: Pick the right four, not just four
md: Many candidates knew that meiosis makes four nuclei and chose four diagrams; only the stronger ones chose the correct four. Work down the list with the two questions rather than counting to four and stopping.

prompt: In the set of six nuclei shown, the parent cell held one long pair and one short pair. Which nucleus could meiosis NOT have produced?
explain: Nucleus (iv) holds both long chromosomes and no short one, so it is missing a whole pair. A meiotic product holds one of each.

text: 6. Why the four are all different

title: GCSE Biology - Meiosis (2027/28 exams)
why: Watch it for the shuffling of the chromosomes, which is the idea this section turns on.

title: What to let pass in that video
md: It is made for another board, so it names the stages of division and shows crossing over. CCEA states that the stages of meiosis and crossing over are not required, so let those parts go by.

**Higher tier.** When the pairs line up before the first division, it is a matter of chance which one of each pair goes to which side. That shuffling is called **independent assortment**, and it is why the four cells are genetically different.

Different gametes mean different offspring. Independent assortment is the source of **variation** in a species.

prompt: Name the process in meiosis that reassorts the chromosomes and so produces variation.
explain: Independent assortment. Examiners report that this term is very rarely written, so it is a cheap mark to secure.

caption: Doubling, not adding. The difference grows fast.

md:
Every round of mitosis **doubles** the number of cells: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 …

So after 5 rounds one cell has become 32, not 10. Count the doublings on your fingers rather than multiplying by the number of divisions.

prompt: One cell divides by mitosis, and every cell it makes then divides again, for 4 rounds of division in all. How many cells are there at the end?

md: This is a late question worth about seven to eleven marks, usually opened by a diagram of a cell and the nuclei that might come from it. The first mark is a number — cells, divisions or chromosomes. The last is normally independent assortment, or a comparison written in full sentences. Stuck? Write the four numbers for each process down the margin and answer from those.
